content: These features enable precise identification of specific points where programmatic interventions can be directed to improve both maternal and perinatal outcomes. The timing of a perinatal death is often the only piece of information available in resource-limited settings, where the burden of disease is highest. This data can be utilized for international comparisons and to guide programmatic decisions, focusing local efforts and interventions effectively. Integrating stillbirth and neonatal death into a standardized system of definitions and coding rules not only ensures comparability but also highlights previously unnoticed deaths, given the widespread use of ICD (adopted by 117 countries for mortality reporting). The ICD-PM system is designed to classify all antepartum, intrapartum, and early neonatal deaths. Early neonatal deaths fall within the perinatal period as defined by ICD-10 and should always be classified using ICD-PM. Late neonatal deaths, while outside the perinatal period, may result from events during the perinatal period. Therefore, the use of ICD-PM for these cases is equally beneficial. Applying ICD-PM principles to late neonatal deaths and linking the conditions of the baby and the mother is valuable from both a classification and programmatic perspective. For instance, in cases of obstructed labor during a term pregnancy leading to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, where neonatal death occurs on day 8, the classification remains consistent with cases where death occurs on day 6. However, there is a subset of late neonatal deaths unrelated to perinatal events, which may not be adequately captured by ICD-PM-linked codes for perinatal deaths. For example, a neonate with an uncomplicated perinatal period who later dies on day 21 from diarrheal illness would fall outside the scope of perinatal classification. The WHO Working Group on Perinatal Death Classification, which developed ICD-PM, decided that ICD-PM should always be used for early neonatal deaths and can be applied to late neonatal deaths. A globally relevant standardized classification system is critical, and ICD-PM has been designed to be applicable in both low-resource settings, where perinatal mortality is highest, and high-resource settings, where mortality is lower but still present across all time periods. The ICD-PM approach allows for the classification of deaths in settings where advanced investigations, such as post-mortem examinations or placental histology, are not feasible. Reporting should be standardized while reflecting local priorities, enabling consistent documentation of perinatal death causes and contributing maternal conditions. The structure of ICD-PM also allows local healthcare facilities, districts, and countries to investigate perinatal deaths based on their specific priorities. This can range from broad-level analysis of timing or ICD-PM groups to detailed extraction of specific causes of death and ICD-10 codes. Training and education are integral to implementing the classification system. During ICD-PM pilot testing, clinicians and researchers not involved in its development were trained in its use. Lessons learned from this process informed further development and the planned rollout of ICD-PM. WHO has also developed the Making Every Baby Count tool for auditing and reviewing stillbirths and neonatal deaths at healthcare facilities. ICD-PM is embedded within this tool and addressed in the associated training and education. The development of ICD-PM involved a consultative process, including a systematic review of over 80 existing classification systems and a Delphi survey of experts from 21 countries, identifying 17 key characteristics necessary for a perinatal death classification system. The Working Group emphasized three main principles: global applicability, adherence to existing ICD-10 rules, and compatibility with the upcoming ICD-11. Pilot testing of ICD-PM on perinatal death databases in South Africa and the United Kingdom demonstrated its applicability, comparability across settings, and utility in identifying areas for targeted interventions to address perinatal mortality. The testing also highlighted areas for improvement in future ICD versions. The first step in capturing perinatal death and maternal condition involves healthcare providers documenting all relevant clinical aspects of the case. This process does not require in-depth knowledge of ICD-10 codes. Once documented, ICD-PM can be applied step-by-step, grouping clinical components into ICD-PM categories and linking them to appropriate ICD-10 codes. The cause of death is determined by a qualified medical practitioner, who uses clinical judgment to complete the medical certificate of cause of death, ensuring all relevant information is recorded comprehensively. WHO provides a perinatal death certificate specific to fetal and maternal conditions, as well as a general death certificate applicable to all deaths. The main disease or condition in the fetus or infant is defined as the underlying cause that initiated the chain of events leading to death. This should be as specific as possible. Additionally, knowing the timing of perinatal death is critical to ICD-PM. The clinical team determines the main maternal condition at the time of perinatal death, which may include conditions such as hypertensive disease in macerated stillbirth or complications during labor and delivery. Even in cases where no maternal condition is identified, this should be explicitly documented to reflect the absence of deviations from standard intrapartum progress. Recording maternal conditions, even in apparently healthy mothers, is essential. For example, a woman with no known conditions during pregnancy who presents with idiopathic preterm labor and whose baby dies from hyaline membrane disease should be documented as having the maternal condition of preterm spontaneous labor with preterm delivery. Linking maternal and perinatal conditions provides valuable information, particularly in settings with limited investigative resources. For instance, in cases of macerated antepartum stillbirth where the mother has tuberculosis, documenting the maternal condition allows for more comprehensive classification of an otherwise unexplained perinatal death. Requiring the recording of maternal conditions also encourages the development of programs and public health policies that benefit both mother and baby. For example, increased antenatal surveillance for hypertension could reduce antepartum stillbirths in cases of pre-eclampsia. Similarly, neonatal deaths following abnormal labor in otherwise healthy mothers could be reduced through targeted interventions.
